rv.q: But there are many times when all of this feels too much, when none of the characters are sufficiently empathetic, when all the shouting and fighting gives you a headache and when you wonder why no one here thought more to leaven the first act with more humor and humanity and truth.
Viterbi's play movingly dives into these questions as it shows the Levi-Katz family celebrating Passover at four dramatically different time periods: The play's first act takes place in 2019.

This late injection of anachronistic whimsy into what has up to now been a realistic family drama — even allowing for its speculative vision of the future — unfortunately, suggests a hokey children’s pageant, undermining the seriousness of Viterbi’s more mature arguments.
A stellar ensemble and a deeply moving script makes In Every Generation a play to remember.
And in the end, this warm story that spans generations is a universal tale of love, caring, acceptance, coping with adversity and achieving one’s goals.
Dillon's subtle, yet always-active portrayal of the aphasic patriarch is breathtaking.
The last scene feels oddly superfluous and anticlimactic, undercutting the tensions that de Mayo and Viterbi build so carefully in the near-dystopian future of 2050.

Overall, I enjoy In Every Generation, but I fear that some will genuinely miss the message if they are not familiar with this historical family tradition. Let's Play Recommends In Every Generation at Victory Gardens Theater.
This challenging Jewish family drama poses a great many questions which the characters don’t always successfully answer or learn from.
The unfortunate and poorly conceived part four is set in the Sinai desert in the year ~1416 BCE, with actors, perhaps the ancestors of the modern-era Levi-Katz clan, speaking English and Italian.
The play appears to want it all ways, and the high volume level and endless histrionics can’t hide the work’s haziness of theme and purpose.
I can tell you that the service can be long and tedious or short and festive... and this question seems to get an answer in this wonderful story.
The play as a whole, while well intended, feels at times unfocused and not leading anywhere in terms of theme and purpose, while also trying too hard to get the point across.

cn.t: Viterbi's family drama thoughtfully explores Jewish identity and intergenerational trauma through Passover seders, earning mostly positive reviews for its timely themes, though some critics find the execution uneven.
